item.title: The farm bill’s existential crisis
item.content:encoded:
Presented by National Pork Producers Council: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin and Grace Yarrow

Presented by 

With help from Marc Heller

“We've come up with a good plan,” committee Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) said in an interview Thursday. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— The farm bill was once a beacon of bipartisanship on Capitol Hill, but this year could mark lawmakers’ fourth consecutive year of failure to clinch a new deal.

— Several major ag industry groups are organizing a sweeping fly-in today and tomorrow, seeking to hit every Senate office.

— The Agriculture Department is seeking to shift how many research grants are funded to leverage more political control over who receives them.

IT’S MONDAY, SEPT. 14. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com and send tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

A message from National Pork Producers Council:

The 60,000+ pork producers we represent need Congress to stop the impending, disastrous patchwork of state laws spurred by California Proposition 12. Without a solution in the farm bill, California — and any other state — can dictate farming practices outside its borders, even from thousands of miles away. Visit fixprop12.com.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

CRACKS IN THE FOUNDATION: The farm bill’s power to rally bipartisan coalitions in Congress is weaker than it’s ever been — and Republicans are running out of time to make the measure relevant again on Capitol Hill.

What was once a must-pass package of agricultural and nutrition policies updated every five years is now niche backburner work for most lawmakers.

A Republican-led proposal for the legislation is floundering in the Senate, raising the prospect of a fourth year of stopgap extensions and another missed opportunity to pass a bill that addresses a struggling farm economy. The stalemate is a sign that the legislation has lost its stature in Congress and that the coalition that sustained it is breaking apart.

That leaves senators confronting an uncomfortable question this week as they return to work and prepare for another attempt to pass Republicans’ version of the legislation: What’s actually in the bill that senators cannot afford to abandon?

“It's a really tough statement on the state of farm bill politics, a pretty blunt reminder of the power and importance of the coalition,” said Jonathan Coppess, a former federal agriculture official who served in senior staff roles in Congress and the Obama administration. “I don't know what more to say other than this is not a good place to be.”

Democrats on the Senate Agriculture Committee voted against Republicans’ farm bill plans during an August markup, furious that the bill didn’t meet their demands to delay a looming deadline for states to start paying for part of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits next year. The panel is set to reconvene this week for another attempt to advance the package.

“We've come up with a good plan,” committee Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) said in an interview Thursday. “And I would really hate for us to put our states in a situation where they come away with nothing, and I think that'll be very difficult for them.”

Democrats’ frustration — and the broader breakdown in the traditional agriculture policy coalition — stems directly from both parties advancing their farm bill priorities through the reconciliation process in recent years.

Republicans already used their domestic policy megabill to pass the most politically valuable policies that are normally part of the farm bill last summer, leaving policy updates without a clear path to become law.

This year's leftover farm bill docket includes a collection of consequential but less urgent policies, such as updates to outdated farm lending limits and changes to major USDA programs. Lawmakers need to pass a new authorization or another extension of the 2018 version of the bill before the end of the year.

If Republicans can’t move the bill with their power trifecta, they risk trying to negotiate it under an even more complicated political climate if Democrats take back a majority in either chamber.

Read the full story from Grace here.
 

Spencer Cox on America’s political divide

In the latest episode of On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Utah Gov. Spencer Cox to discuss his new book, Off Ramp, the future of the Republican Party, immigration reform and what he says it will take to rebuild trust and community in American life.

Watch now.

 
 
On the Hill

BOOZMAN’S FORECAST: Boozman told MA he expects ag groups to keep pressure on lawmakers ahead of the next farm bill vote.

“They have been putting pressure on not just Democrats, but also making sure that the support is there on the Republican side in getting this done,” he said in the interview. “I would really encourage the farm community to continue to reach out and give different examples of the policies that are in there, such as increasing loan limits and things that really would help them a great deal.”

Boozman also told MA he is hoping to hold a hearing during the next three weeks to advance two Trump nominees to the Farm Credit Administration: John Grunewald of Oklahoma and Carl Bednarski of Michigan.

“We want to clear those out as quickly as we can,” Boozman said. “As far as I can tell, they're not controversial at all.”
 

A message from National Pork Producers Council:
 

SHOE LEATHER: The American Farm Bureau Federation has organized a massive fly-in this week alongside other key commodity groups, with the goal of visiting every Senate office to discuss agriculture policy.

The participating organizations include the National Corn Growers Association, the American Soybean Association, USA Rice, the National Association of Wheat Growers, the Farm Credit Council, the American Bankers Association and the National Sorghum Producers.

The organizations’ members will be on the Hill Monday and Tuesday.

A message from National Pork Producers Council:

Passing a bipartisan farm bill is essential. Republicans and Democrats agree: Congress must save family farms by fixing California Proposition 12.

Prop. 12 causes damaging consequences nationwide by:
· Trampling on states’ rights and undermining the foundation of interstate commerce, allowing one state to mandate farming practices outside its borders — even from thousands of miles away.
· Increasing industry consolidation and reducing competition, threatening the livelihood of small farmers who are less likely to be able to afford the high costs of rebuilding their barns when another state passes a conflicting law.
· Ignoring veterinary advice and chipping away at sound animal care options.
· Increasing prices at the grocery store as much as 41% for pork products.

America’s pork producers need the Senate to pass a farm bill that stops the reckless Prop. 12 patchwork of state-by-state laws.

For bacon’s sake, pass the farm bill!

fixprop12.com
 
Around the Agencies

GRANT BATTLE: The federal government has long awarded agricultural research grants to universities based on set criteria, such as how many farmers live in the states where the schools are located.

But the Trump administration has a problem with that formula: It was written by Congress.

USDA is proposing to cut or eliminate hundreds of millions of dollars in grants based on calculations set in law. Instead, USDA officials want Congress to put more money toward competitive grants that the department directly controls.

The push against formula grants comes alongside a broader effort by the administration to change how all federal grants are awarded or canceled, handing more authority to political appointees who will ensure funding decisions align with President Donald Trump’s priorities.

Colleges and universities are pushing back, pressing lawmakers to reject the administration's fiscal 2027 proposals, which could cut off a significant stream of research funding. At the same time, they’re afraid of pitting formula grants against competitive ones, arguing both are essential to keeping the United States a world leader in agricultural science.

The formula grants cover basic, long-term research on subjects like crop science — the building blocks that allow researchers to turn to competitive grants for more groundbreaking work, said Doug Steele, senior vice president for food, agriculture and natural resources at the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities, which represents public research institutions.

“We call it pivot money,” Steele said, explaining how formula grants set the stage for competitive grants. “We don’t believe that there’s some kind of competition. Both are important.”

Each state and the District of Columbia have at least one land-grant college, which is designated by Congress or state legislatures to receive federal funding for agriculture or related research. North Carolina State and Texas A&M, for example, each received about $9 million in Hatch Act funding in fiscal 2025.

Read the full story from Marc here.
 

Where energy, tech and policy connect

POLITICO Surge helps readers follow the policy and political forces behind data center growth, rising electricity demand, infrastructure pressure and the energy transition.

Subscribe Now.

 
 
Row Crops

— Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins will speak at the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture’s annual meeting in Portland, Maine, on Wednesday.

— The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the nation’s largest-ever outbreak of cyclospora illnesses is over, as of Friday, as our Marcia Brown reported.

— Former West Virginia state Sen. Paul Hardesty has been on Ag Committee Sen. Jim Justice’s (R-W.Va.) payroll while registered to lobby the state legislature on behalf of tobacco company Altria since January 2025, as our Jacob Wendler reported.

— The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office recommended the Trump administration conduct a sweeping assessment of the threats disease and pests pose to forests and the agriculture industry, as Grace reported.

— The United Nations is set to appoint Luke Lindberg, USDA’s undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs, as executive director of the United Nations’ World Food Program. (The Hagstrom Report)

item.title: Bull’s-eye on Big Ag
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

With help from Amanda Chu and Samuel Benson

Candidates running to represent ag-heavy states have unleashed a flood of populist messaging that blames conglomerates for squeezing U.S. farmers and unfairly fixing prices. | Charlie Neibergall/AP
QUICK FIX

— Rural midterms candidates are tapping into farm community rancor against agricultural conglomerates.

— Vice President JD Vance wooed rural and agricultural voters on behalf of Iowa Republicans.

— Corporate America is paying for access to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

IT’S MONDAY, SEPT. 21. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com and send me tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

BREAK IT UP: A common villain has emerged across party lines in rural America: Big Ag.

Candidates running to represent ag-heavy states have unleashed a flood of populist messaging that blames conglomerates for squeezing U.S. farmers and unfairly fixing prices. Farmers have long been a reliable voting bloc for Republicans, but insurgents are trying to loosen that grip.

They are naming corporations that produce seeds, chemicals and fertilizer as adversaries despite those corporations typically spending exorbitantly on political races and wielding considerable influence in Washington.

The attacks come after Make America Healthy Again activists led an ultimately unsuccessful fight to block preemptions that would protect Bayer — the German-based conglomerate that makes the widely used herbicide Roundup — against legal liability related to the product’s cancer warning labeling.

“Our farmers are getting kicked in the teeth over and over and over again and they need help, and they're starting to see that our federal delegation is just taking the money and doing the bidding of the companies,” independent Nebraska Senate nominee Dan Osborn told MA. “I have a problem with the big corporations in ag and the fact that they're the ones receiving most of the subsidies.”

The messaging pattern comes as farmers weather a bout of trade conflict with Canada, while poor financial conditions like high input costs and low commodity prices persist.

Farmers who spoke with MA said their plight isn’t bad luck but the product of a political and economic system stacked against them.

“There's not any region of the country that's feeling the pain of this monopoly power, this extractive economic model that they have, more than rural America, and it's playing out in our pocketbooks,” said Joe Maxwell, president of Farm Action Fund and a Missouri farmer. “Sixty-three farmers a day are going out of business, and families can't afford their food.”

“The Bayers, the JBS’s, write a $5 million check to inaugural funds,” Maxwell added. “All this money, all this influence. But at some point, folks get pissed off, and they begin to push back.”

Multiple rural candidates are seeking to establish themselves as disruptors of the political economy they say is tilted in favor of special interests, including Iowa Republican gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn.

“I've been hearing this for years — I just have not been hearing people on the political side talking about it or taking it seriously,” Lahn told your host. “You have farmers that have finally found a voice in candidates or some politicians that believe that we can make a difference here.”

Lahn pointed to Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, Nutrien and Koch as offenders. He said he wants to stop tax incentives for companies that are “participating in the consolidation of our agriculture input market” and divert the money to local businesses that compete with big names.

IN RELATED NEWS: Farm-state Republicans don’t support President Donald Trump’s move to import cheap beef, but they’re still getting grilled for it.

Trump’s plan to combat sky-high beef prices by introducing discounted, tariff-free foreign beef has been widely condemned by ag-state Republicans who are concerned it will undercut the domestic beef industry and hurt ranchers. Their opponents see an opening to paint Republicans as unconcerned about voters’ pocketbook concerns.

Osborn’s campaign went on air with a pun-filled ad this week in which he says the import plan is “selling out American farmers and ranchers” and blasts Congress for being “too chicken to stand up to the corporations who bought them off.”

The campaign says it plans to spend at least six figures airing the spot. It’s the first major spending from a campaign focused on the beef import plan. But it plays into a larger economic argument GOP opponents are pushing to break through with farmers and ranchers: Trump and Republicans have turned their backs on rural America as a worsening farm crisis and spiking fuel and fertilizer prices pinch agricultural communities.

“It’s part of a wider frustration,” said an adviser to a farm-state GOP senator, granted anonymity to speak openly. “I don’t think it sways anyone’s vote, but it isn’t a great look. … It isn’t fun for me to read the headline. It’s frustrating.”

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Osborn’s opponent, said in a statement he has a record of standing for his state’s agriculture community, “no matter who is president — from fighting Biden’s 30x30 plan to opposing this beef import plan.”

“Ranchers know the difference between a senator who delivers and a candidate reading a script his socialist ad agency wrote,” Ricketts said.

Read more from Sam here.
Midterms Watch

Vice President JD Vance spoke in support of Iowa Republicans Friday. | Getty Images

ON THE TRAIL: Vance focused on farm issues while stumping in Iowa on Friday for Lahn and ginning up support for other Republicans, including Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig.

The veep spoke extensively about protecting ownership of Iowa farmland, saying Lahn would “take on the corporations and the foreign buyers who treat Iowa farmland like it’s at sale for auction.”

Vance touted the Trump administration’s work opening new foreign markets for ag commodities but steered clear of Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran, which have hiked production costs.

“We now have, thanks to Donald Trump’s hard work and fighting on behalf of Iowa farmers, 2 billion new consumers all over the world who are now open to American food,” Vance said. “Markets that were closed to our beef and dairy for decades are taking Iowa beef and dairy today.”

Vance pointed to a provision of the GOP megalaw that permanently allows people to inherit up to $15 million tax-free, saying the estate tax law would improve the cost of doing business for farmers.

“We got to make it more affordable to actually grow things here and we got to get Washington out of the way of our great farmers, and that's why we made the death tax exemption permanent,” Vance said. “Because we did not want Washington to try to steal your farm when you try to pass your farm from one generation to the next.”

But Vance largely avoided addressing economic conditions depressing farmers’ livelihoods, including eye-popping diesel prices that are concerning Republican farm-state lawmakers. He took aim at Democrats, including Lahn’s opponent Rob Sand and figures in the national spotlight, such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico.
Influence and Industry

THE ACCESS GAME: When devotees of the MAHA movement meet for a summit Sept. 29 in Washington, titans of American industry will pay the bill.

Walmart, America’s biggest retailer and a leading purveyor of the ultraprocessed foods MAHA decries, is among the sponsors. So are two artificial intelligence giants, OpenAI and Anthropic, whose chief executives recently asked Washington to regulate them in order to prevent their tools from wiping out humanity.

In exchange, they’ll get to attend a private dinner with summit speakers, which include Health and Human Services Department officials. Other sponsors are less well known, but also have interests before Kennedy’s department, including makers of psychedelic drugs, diagnostics technologies and peptides that need government approval.

The MAHA movement’s embrace of corporate sponsorship runs counter to its anti-corporate message: that the food and health care industries have knowingly poisoned Americans’ health, causing obesity, vaccine injuries and chronic disease.

MAHA PAC, its political fundraising arm, has also accepted large donations from companies. A POLITICO analysis of MAHA PAC filings from January 2025 to April 2026 found almost 90% of its donations came from just 10 entities, half of which have ties to the drug industry.

Tony Lyons, whose MAHA Center is putting on the summit, galvanizes supporters on weekly calls with warnings about “dark forces” in industry threatening Kennedy’s agenda.

“Our doctors, along with the government agencies and the media, were bribed, conflicted, coerced, until they didn’t know or care what the truth was. They all became marketing arms, sort of co-conspirators for the very companies making us sick and keeping us sick for profit,” he said Wednesday.

“The forces that are lined up against all of you are just monstrous. These are just such powerful forces with such powerful lobbyists,” he added.

Lyons did not respond to POLITICO’s requests for comment.

Read Amanda’s full story here.
Row Crops

— For food companies, shifts from GLP-1 use are hard to adapt to. (The New York Times)

— What commodity markets can expect from the Trump-Xi summit. (Reuters)

— Americans spend more time cooking than they have in two decades, but hectic schedules and rising costs make it a key pain point. (The Wall Street Journal)

item.title: Grim farm aid outlook
item.content:encoded:
Presented by ADM: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by ADM

With help from Marcia Brown and Oliver Ward

“If it doesn’t get in the farmers’ hands until 2027, we’re just going to lose a whole bunch more folks,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) said. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— Ag Republicans lamented that additional farm aid won’t move until at least the lame-duck period, likely not reaching farmers before spring 2027.

— The “stage is set” for a trade deal between the United States and Mexico, with ag products a part of the talks.

— Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins was among the best primed to operate in President Donald Trump’s second-term Cabinet.

IT’S MONDAY, SEPT. 28. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com and send tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from ADM:

Resilience begins on the farm. By improving and protecting soil health, farmers are better positioned to adapt to changing conditions and maintain production. These regenerative farming practices aren’t new for America’s farmers. But for regen ag to continue to grow, it needs to be scaled—and valued. ADM’s re:generations™ program connects thousands of farmers with tools, incentives and market demand, helping strengthen American agriculture and the soil farmers depend on. Learn more.
 
Driving the day

BETTER LATE THAN NEVER? Ag Republicans say the timeline for getting additional economic aid to farmers is moving too slow, with growers pushed to the financial brink by factors like the Iran war and the trade war with Canada.

“If it doesn’t get in the farmers’ hands until 2027, we’re just going to lose a whole bunch more folks,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) told MA. “Every day we wait and everything causes more stress and more farm closures.

“The only problem is this place moves like a snail and you can't get it to move like a rabbit,” he added, referring to Congress.

Republicans want to lump in about $11 billion in direct farm aid with a forthcoming defense spending package. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said Thursday that the farm aid would “ride along pretty easily if we get that money for the military.”

But even if that measure clears Congress, there would be a delay before checks hit farmers’ bank accounts, likely around spring of 2027. That might come too late to save some farmers’ businesses after a brutal harvest season amid record-breaking diesel prices.

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) told MA that Republicans hope to pass farm aid “soon in the lame duck” and that he thinks it will draw some Democratic support. But he added that farmers “needed it yesterday.”

“This is a generational crisis where, unless we step in, we’re going to lose a lot of our farmers, which ultimately will raise food prices significantly,” Boozman said.

“[Trump] is very much engaged at this point with pushing the farm bill through and farm aid,” he added. The farm bill cleared the Senate Ag Committee earlier this month but will likely not get a floor vote before midterms.

Kevin Studer, vice president of government relations at the Iowa Corn Growers Association, said even though the money from a lame-duck supplemental would be delivered on a delayed time frame, banks would acknowledge that more money is on the way.

“Everything is about, in the farming community, keeping the bankers happy,” Studer said, adding that if Congress passes more direct aid, then bankers will “be more willing to work with that producer for another year.”
 

A message from ADM:
 
TRADE TALKS

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said earlier this month that trade talks with the United States have been progressing and that she spoke with Trump directly by phone. | Pool photo by Mandel Ngan

LOOKING FOR A WIN: The Trump administration is trying to achieve trade progress to tout ahead of the midterm elections, prompting a turn to Mexico amid the trade war with Canada and a temporary trade truce with China, Oliver writes in.

The United States has made clear to Mexican officials that it wants to announce an early harvest deal before the midterms, according to a Mexican industry figure briefed on the status of negotiations and granted anonymity to discuss them.

The two sides have been talking as part of the six-year review of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the free trade deal underpinning North American trade. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told lawmakers in July that he was aiming to secure an interim deal with Mexico before the end of the year.

“There's not much else to cover,” said the industry figure, adding that “the stage is set” for a deal.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said earlier this month the talks have been progressing and that she spoke with Trump directly by phone to move a deal along.

What’s left? In recent weeks, Mexico has announced several steps to ameliorate long-standing U.S. trade complaints. In late August, Sheinbaum's government proposed new steps to vet foreign investments in sensitive industries.

Officials also earlier this month launched an aluminum import monitoring program, upgraded the country’s steel import monitoring efforts and proposed a cut in the fees charged for radio spectrum.

In return, the U.S. has offered Mexico the “most preferential treatment on tariffs vis-a-vis the rest of the world,” the industry official said.

The fourth round of bilateral negotiations, which was supposed to kick off this week, has been postponed. But officials are hoping the next round will be the last and that a deal will be ready to announce in the coming weeks.

Some sticking points remain, particularly around agriculture, according to three people familiar with the talks, granted anonymity to discuss them.

Lawmakers have pushed U.S. officials to address seasonal imports of fruits and vegetables that compete with U.S. growers during their harvest periods, but the U.S. and Mexico have not agreed on a path forward, the people said.

“Both sides are pressing the other to actually paper text," one of the people said.

Similarly, the U.S. wants to secure protections for some generic meat and cheese names. But this could upend a Mexico-European Union deal, in which the former pledged to protect European names for hundreds of products, limiting the use of terms like feta and Manchego to specific European regions.

USTR did not respond to a request for comment on the state of negotiations.
 

A message from ADM:

Regenerative agriculture has to work both on the farm and across the value chain. ADM brings American farmers and customers together to help protect our soil and strengthen American agriculture, outcomes, backed by our unparallelled operational footprint connecting growers to growing market demand.

In 2025, ADM’s re:generations™ program engaged more than 3,000 U.S. farmers across approximately 3.8 million acres, 8 crops and 22 states with market opportunities for what they grew, including nearly 250,000 acres of wheat in the U.S. In a survey of program farmers, 91% of farmers said the program had a positive impact on their farm economics, and 99% said they plan to re-enroll.

Learn more about how ADM is helping increase value for farmers.
 
AT THE WHITE HOUSE

CABINET OF CURIOSITIES: Among all the new figures crowded around Trump’s second-term Cabinet table, Rollins was among the best-prepared to navigate the coming four years. As head of Trump’s first-term Domestic Policy Council, she had an up-close view of the way the president cycled through top officials, with frequent firings and high-profile resignations that contributed to what one think tank characterized as record Cabinet turnover.

Rollins’ communication style reflects her new job. In public pronouncements, Rollins often describes moving at “Trump speed” and takes pains to cheer on the president’s work on matters far from her domain, such as his handling of a contentious meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.

In her office at USDA’s headquarters, a map of the U.S. with pushpins documenting her official travels includes a post-it note scrawled with “America” atop the original topographical labeling of Gulf of Mexico.

Rollins learned to convey important information to Trump via visual aids, a preferred medium of communication she shared with a president who has little interest in dense written material. She brought a graphic designer’s eye to the materials she could hold up for television cameras outside the White House while defending the administration against accusations it was responsible for soaring egg prices during her first weeks in office.

That early messaging blitz — including a series of charts Rollins had her staff perfect with typographical changes like bolding and larger font, along with an upgrade from flimsy paper to larger card stock — paid off with her most important viewer as she touted a drop in egg prices.

“The egg prices, they were going through the sky,” Trump said, addressing Rollins as he rolled out a slate of tariffs in April 2025. “And you did a fantastic job. Now we have lots of eggs, and they’re much cheaper.”

Rollins also entered the Cabinet with a clear idea of how to approach her colleagues, many of whom she knew personally from having worked together at her think tank or elsewhere in Republican politics.

During the first term, Rollins saw what could go wrong. There was infighting, in which rivals undercut one another in the press and behind each other’s back to Trump, and rival factions inside the administration slowed the real work of governing.

Read more from Marcia and our White House colleagues in POLITICO Magazine.
Row Crops

— Alexandra Fasulo has no training in farming or professional background in energy policy, but she’s emerged as a power player in the fight over solar on farmland, our Marie J. French reports.

— The Texas Cattle Feeders Association, the Kansas Livestock Association and the Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association said in a joint statement that ICE operations in their states are disrupting ranchers’ businesses.

— Trump administration officials are weighing alternatives to imposing a ban on diesel exports to bring prices for the fuel down from record highs — including passing the issue down to the state level, our Ben Lefebvre and Meredith Lee Hill report.

— Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Chris Jones, a retired research scientist, for Iowa agriculture secretary, saying Jones would “stand up to big agriculture.” (Des Moines Register)

Presented by Bayer: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Bayer

Decoded by POLITICO Launches Today

The future of the world is being dictated in real time by the intersection of tech titans and governments. But there's just way too much tech news to monitor.

Your inboxes are full. Your feeds are even fuller. Push alerts pile up. And your phones won’t stop pinging. Every hour brings another headline about artificial intelligence breakthroughs and hacks, regulatory fights across the 50 states and global capitals, huge donations to super PACs by tech titans and even bigger IPOs, the stampede of political consultants and lobbyists to tech, policy prescriptions, and ambitious politicians scrambling to keep pace with exhausted and increasingly alarmed voters.

That’s where Decoded by POLITICO comes in.

We’re not here to add another stream to the feed. We’re here to help you find the signal. Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast debut today with an exclusive interview with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who told our Brendan Bordelon he believes “the world should accept some bad things happening” for the benefits of AI. Altman also delved into President Donald Trump’s new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted “super intelligence” rebrand, the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability, Altman’s thoughts on the AI industry money swamping U.S. politics, and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Decoded cuts through the churn to focus on the people, policy fights and political battles reshaping tech — and, increasingly, the world around it. Anchored by Brendan, Calder McHugh, Christine Mui and Sam Sutton, and drawing on the reporting of nearly 50 POLITICO journalists across the world, Decoded tells you what happened, why it matters, who is gaining — and losing — influence, and what comes next — without making you slog through everything that happened along the way.

Because the challenge isn’t finding information. It’s knowing what’s actually changing in tech politics and policy — and where power is moving — so you can act before the shift becomes obvious.

We hope you’ll sign up, subscribe to the pod, and share your feedback.

— Christopher Cadelago, executive editor for Global Technology and California

Soybeans were left off a deal cut by the U.S. and China that included a list of tariff exemptions for U.S. ag commodities. | Rodrigo Abd/AP

With help from Amanda Chu
QUICK FIX

— Soybeans are “notably absent” from a list of tariff-exempted ag exports after the U.S.-China summit.

— The leading organizer of the Make America Healthy Again movement promised to raise $100 million to support Republicans this year. He’s nowhere close.

— The Food and Drug Administration announced a strategy to prevent cyclospora outbreaks next year.

IT’S MONDAY, OCT. 5. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Contact me at rshin@politico.com and send tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

At Bayer, we believe in delivering smart, practical tools directly to American farmers. Through advanced digital platforms, we provide accurate, real-time data maps with insights on moisture, nutrients, and compaction. This gives farmers the information they need to unlock their soil's full potential. We empower growers to advance regenerative agriculture, helping to secure a financially sustainable future with boosted yields. Learn more.
 
Driving the day

WHO’S BEAN EXCLUDED? The deal cut by President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in September included a list of tariff exemptions for U.S. ag commodities. One crop was conspicuously left off.

Soybean exports from the United States will still face a 10% retaliatory tariff from Beijing, which the industry said was disheartening and Republican lawmakers hope will be relitigated.

“We were disappointed because we were hoping that they would be exempted from the 10% retaliatory duty that still remains in place,” American Soybean Association CEO Stephen Censky told MA. “We thought this would improve the competitive position for soybeans long-term, and we're still going to keep on pressing for this.”

China has already committed to buying 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans in each of the next three years as part of a previous agreement following Beijing’s monthslong boycott of American soybeans. Republicans urged the Trump administration to raise the point in future meetings with China.

“Notably absent from the list of products for tariff reduction is soybeans to China,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told reporters Wednesday. “I'm going to continue to push the administration to reduce Chinese tariffs on this agriculture product.”

China and the U.S. agreed at the summit that they will establish an ag working group to discuss trade barriers to U.S. ag products.

The leaders have two more meetings on the calendar later this year in which they could hash out unresolved issues, including easing duties on soybeans. Xi and Trump plan to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China, in November and at the G20 meeting in Miami in December.

The 10% tariff functions to essentially block U.S. soybean sales to China’s lucrative private sector, Censky said, because it makes the product much more expensive than foreign competitors’ prices. Most of the product Beijing already agreed to buy will flow through state-operated companies, and it’s not clear whether those enterprises are also paying the tariff, Censky said.

“I would always like to see tariffs on agricultural products come down,” Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) told MA Thursday. “What we need to do right now is make sure communist China lives up to their obligations to buy the soybeans.”

China has fulfilled at least 11 million of its 25 million metric ton soybean purchase commitment for this year, according to the Agriculture Department’s export sale reports.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said he spoke with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer about soybeans last week and that Greer said he was satisfied with Beijing’s purchasing schedule.

“They're on track, and [Greer] feels they will complete that,” Hoeven told MA Thursday. “He would tell you they're doing well and that they're not adding additional tariffs on there and it's just the 10% that was there before.”

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not respond to a request for comment.
 

A message from Bayer:
 
Around the Agencies

Cyclospora-contaminated iceberg lettuce sickened thousands this summer. | AP

PREVENTION TACTICS: The FDA announced it plans to release a report detailing its investigation into the summer’s cyclospora outbreak and will boost surveillance to prevent future surges of the parasite.

As part of a release explaining its next steps to prevent cyclospora outbreaks in 2027, the agency said it will increase inspections of foreign produce suppliers and conduct public outreach efforts to increase awareness about food safety best practices.

The FDA said it will also work with the Mexican government to strengthen cyclospora prevention practices in the country’s produce supply chain and implement new data sources and tools to monitor environmental factors that could contribute to the parasite’s spread.

The agency said the forthcoming report will “summarize the outbreak investigation [and] review the potential factors contributing to the contamination of imported, shredded iceberg lettuce.” The report will be published ahead of the 2027 growing season, the FDA wrote.

You will recall: This summer’s multistate cyclospora outbreak sickened thousands of people, hospitalizing more than a thousand. As the outbreak raged, the Trump administration shuttered research projects on the parasite, as Marcia Brown and your host reported.

The hollowing-out of three cyclospora projects — two which were defunded by Congress and one which is subject to reorganization — is expected to hinder future research progress on the parasite.

When farmers are equipped to care for their soil with tools like real-data maps, stronger yields and a sustainable bottom line naturally follow.

Learn more.
 
MAHA WATCH

A HOUSE NOT IN ORDER: A month before the midterms, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA movement is in disarray, Amanda reports.

MAHA PAC, the movement's political financing arm, has had fewer than 20 donors this year, totalling just $1 million, filings show. That’s far short of the $100 million PAC leader Tony Lyons committed to support Republicans in the midterm elections.

The PAC has spent less than $800,000 to support candidates this year, according to the filings. No money went to races that will help Republicans maintain control of Congress, frustrating MAHA supporters who worry leaders are squandering the movement’s momentum after it helped return Trump to office.

“What a joke!” Alex Clark, a MAHA influencer who works at the conservative group Turning Point USA said of the PAC’s spending. “We're talking about millions of voters who just fell into our lap like manna from heaven, and we're just gonna let them walk away.”

Lyons, who leads a web of MAHA nonprofits and political groups, did not respond to requests for comment. He galvanizes supporters on weekly calls about the “dark forces” of corporate lobbyists threatening to undermine Kennedy’s agenda.

MAHA PAC’s donors, however, are often companies that have interests before the Health Department, POLITICO reported in April. The PAC’s latest fundraising report came as Lyons hosted an invite-only summit in Washington that drew large corporate sponsors, from OpenAI to Walmart.

“These outside entities that have branded themselves as representative of the MAHA voting bloc … they are not helping us,” said Stephanie Stock, who was backed by one of Lyons’ MAHA nonprofits in a failed run for state House in Ohio earlier this year. She received no funding from Lyons’ groups.

Splinters: Frustration with leadership marks the movement’s latest fracture. Supporters have repeatedly expressed disillusionment since February, when Trump protected a pesticide MAHA supporters have long sought to eliminate.

They are also divided over which party MAHA belongs to. While Lyons has pledged to only support Republicans, other prominent MAHA voices are straying.

Zen Honeycutt, founder of nonprofit Moms Across America, recently rallied candidates supportive of MAHA at a convention for political independents. Her nonprofit plans to support 20 candidates across party lines.

“That's not what some of the people in the MAHA world would want from us. They want us to align with the Republican Party, but we will talk to anyone,” she said, calling MAHA “nonpartisan.”

Some fear the divisions will hurt their chances in November. “Unless they all come together, they're just splintering,” said one state organizer granted anonymity out of fear of retaliation. “You’re not going to get the person in.”

Presented by Bayer: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Bayer

With help from Marcia Brown and Mia McCarthy

President Donald Trump announced an executive order that waives the off-road requirement for purchasing tax-free red-dyed diesel. | Jacquelyn Martin/AP
QUICK FIX

— Fruit and vegetable growers are under particular strain from sky-high diesel costs.

— Calley Means has transferred posts in the Trump administration.

— Walmart rebutted a former Democratic aide's claims on price gouging.

IT’S TUESDAY, OCT. 6. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Contact me at rshin@politico.com and send tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we empower American farms with the smart tools needed to advance regenerative agriculture. By providing accurate, real-time data maps, we give farmers necessary insights to improve soil health and protect the land for generations. When farmers are equipped to care for their soil with tools like real-data maps, stronger yields and a sustainable bottom line naturally follow. Learn more.
 
Driving the day

BRUISED FRUIT: High diesel prices are pummeling fresh produce growers, who say their growing cost crisis will soon be passed on to consumers’ wallets without some form of relief.

Specialty crops such as apples, blueberries and other fresh foods are particularly sensitive to fuel prices, leaving their growers hit especially hard since the Iran war rocked energy markets and spiked diesel prices to record-breaking levels.

The industry is now waiting to see whether an executive order from President Donald Trump, announced Monday evening, lowers diesel prices in a meaningful way. The order, which Trump signed at a Nebraska rally, temporarily waives the off-road requirement for purchasing tax-free red-dyed diesel. The fuel is already widely used in the ag economy.

“I don't know what the hell it is, but whatever it is, it's supposed to be very good,” Trump said of red-dyed diesel. “The typical trucker will save over $100 every time they fill up. ... And farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars.”

But there is debate about whether widening red-dyed diesel access will soften farmers’ costs. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracker GasBuddy, wrote on social media last week that “farmers already use dyed diesel and are still paying record prices.”

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins urged states earlier Monday to take action to ease diesel prices through lower taxes, and she credited states that have already made temporary changes to fuel policy, such as Arkansas, for providing relief.

The produce industry said its sector is disproportionately affected by the fuel’s cost because fresh fruits and vegetables must be shipped to stores almost immediately.

“The lifespan of most perishable product is under a week from the time it's cut in the field to on a grocery store shelf and purchased by an American family,” said Samantha Ayoub, director of workforce and business policy at the International Fresh Produce Association.

“All of that, from the minute it comes out of the field until the minute it's in your home, is run basically on diesel,” she added.

Petroleum’s effect on expenses throughout the fruit and vegetable supply chain are not isolated to shipping, Ayoub said. Fresh produce often must be continuously refrigerated. It is also often sold in clamshell containers made from plastic — which is derived from petroleum.

Elevated diesel prices will result in higher consumer prices if the situation continues, said Adam Lytch, a vegetable producer and chair of the Florida Fruit & Vegetable Association.

“The costs are certainly up, and quite honestly, we're going to have to get more for the products because of it,” Lytch told MA Monday.

Lytch said for his vegetable farm, he must truck in more than 250 semi-loads of plants and seed to grow his crop, separate from the truckloads of produce that get shipped to stores, calling the price tally “scary.”

“We don't have the luxury of being able to hold and wait for better markets. Our items must go,” he added.
ON THE HILL

WAIVER ASK: Agriculture Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) is undeterred in wanting a waiver to continue as the panel’s top Republican — despite skepticism from some in his party, Mia writes in.

A number of current and possible future GOP Steering Committee members have criticized the handful of chairs asking to extend their roles beyond the six-year term limit, which the party has had in place for decades. Thompson noted that those members are also able to apply for a waiver to stay on the influential steering panel that will ultimately dole out extensions.

“We provide waivers to be on the Steering Committee," Thompson said in an interview. “There's no limitations on that, so it's sort of an interesting paradox."

Thompson also said he intends to seek a waiver whether House Republicans are in the majority or not. He added that he does not believe that the increased number of chairs applying for a waiver will hurt his chances of getting one: “The Republican Party has always been one of merit,” he said.

"It's opportunity and leadership earned,” Thompson told Mia. “And I think I've done that above and beyond with the Agriculture Committee.”
MAHA MOMENT

NEW OFFICE DIGS: Means, one of the most visible government spokespeople for the Make America Healthy Again movement, is no longer a senior adviser at the White House, Marcia and Carmen Paun confirmed.

Means, who started in the Trump administration as a special government employee, was on a detail at the White House from the Department of Health and Human Services, where he is now a senior adviser. His detail ended this summer.

“He has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement confirming the change.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard called Means a “fearless advocate” for the MAHA movement.

The move doesn’t change Means’ role as an advocate for MAHA issues within government, such as removing soda from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or advocating to eliminate synthetic food dyes, said a person familiar with the situation, granted anonymity to discuss internal personnel issues.
 

A message from Bayer:
 
INDUSTRY CORNER

FOOD FIGHT: Walmart is pushing back against claims by a former aide to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) that the company is using new technology to price-gouge customers, Marcia reports.

Dan Bartlett, Walmart’s executive vice president for corporate affairs, demanded Monday that consumer advocate Lindsay Owens publicly "correct the record," saying that she has repeatedly mischaracterized the company's business strategies.

Owens, CEO of the progressive nonprofit Groundwork Collaborative, has said in interviews promoting her new book that Walmart is using dynamic pricing and consumer data to squeeze shoppers and has plans to deploy artificial intelligence-driven tools that could elevate prices.

“Walmart does not and will not use an individual customer’s personal information, income, shopping history, urgency or willingness to pay to set an individualized price,” Bartlett said in a letter posted on the company’s website. “Hold us accountable to that promise, but do so based on what we actually do and not what you’ve decided we could possibly do.”

The letter, which comes a week after Walmart’s CEO made a similar argument, is the latest in an increasingly hostile battle over new pricing technologies. The issue has drawn bipartisan scrutiny and comes as inflation for ordinary goods like groceries frustrates American consumers.

House lawmakers have opened an inquiry into surveillance pricing practices that they say can artificially inflate consumer prices. The Federal Trade Commission recently proposed a new enforcement policy for how consumer data can be used in pricing, and Maryland recently became the first state to ban dynamic pricing in grocery stores.

Owens has criticized Walmart while promoting her recently published book, “Gouged,” which contends that Americans “are getting ripped off” through extra fees, dynamic pricing and exploiting consumer data.

"The confusion around Walmart's pricing practices is of its own making," Owens said in a statement to POLITICO, calling Walmart's attacks "baseless."

She added, "My life's work is studying and improving Americans' financial well-being. I welcome a conversation with anyone who desires to do the same."

Walmart said it will not use its recently launched digital shelf labels to take advantage of consumer needs, such as by “raising prices in response to a hot afternoon or an approaching snowstorm.”

Bartlett’s letter disputes Owens’ suggestion that Walmart uses technology to do things like raise the price of mayonnaise once a shopper has put tuna in their digital cart and denies her claim that the company uses its AI shopping assistant “Sparky” to upcharge customers.

item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin and Marcia Brown

With help from Cassandra Dumay

EDITOR'S NOTE: Due to a production error, last week you received editions of Weekly Agriculture on both Monday and Tuesday. We hope you enjoyed the additional newsletter typically reserved for our Pro subscribers.

Avian flu has stricken 2 million birds just in the last three months. | Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vaccine views helped stall an internal Agriculture Department bird flu inoculation strategy.

— USDA’s Rural Development arm is lagging on its multifamily homes spending.

— A new report finds that states are well short of what they need to fund the new administrative costs for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

IT’S TUESDAY, OCT. 13. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! We’re your hosts, Rachel Shin and Marcia Brown. Send pitches to rshin@politico.com and send tips securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
Driving the day

THE BEST-LAID PLANS: Kennedy’s anti-vaccine views were a major factor in shelving a USDA avian flu response plan, according to five people with direct knowledge of the matter, a pause that’s alarming lawmakers as wild birds begin migrating for the winter. 

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins rolled out a $1 billion five-point plan in February 2025 to tackle a record-breaking spread of avian influenza. The disease has roiled the poultry industry since 2022, killing about 200 million birds and contributing to record-high egg prices last year.

Rollins later pulled back on an internal USDA strategy for vaccinating poultry and egg-laying hens initially intended to be shared widely with foreign countries and industry leaders. It's not clear whether Kennedy urged Rollins to halt the plan, but she was concerned about whether it would clash with the Health secretary's anti-vaccine views, according to the five people, all of whom were granted anonymity to discuss the internal dynamics.

Rollins was also dealing with industry tension between egg producers who favor vaccination and meat producers concerned that inoculating chickens could hurt their ability to export. She also faced less pressure to act as egg prices fell from record levels.

Still, the pause, which went against the counsel of expert agency staff and industry leaders, continues to raise alarm among USDA employees because its other efforts to stamp out the virus have so far failed. The decision is also at odds with calls from Republican lawmakers to ensure the United States is prepared for a potential surge in cases this fall.

“It's time to get a vaccine in place, but it's also time to address the issue with our trading partners,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said in an interview. “We are being caught flat-footed, and we are losing millions of birds per year right now, which is driving up the price for protein.”

President Donald Trump bashed the Biden administration over egg prices on the campaign trail in 2024, only to see them continuing to rise as bird flu raged early in his second term.

“Eggs became so symbolic, almost like gasoline,” said Kevin Shea, a former administrator of the USDA agency that manages bird flu outbreaks.

Read the full story from your host and Marcia here.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

RURAL HOUSING FUNDS LANGUISH: USDA’s Rural Development agency is falling behind on rural housing spending for multifamily homes.

For fiscal 2024 through fiscal 2026, Congress gave the agency more than $157 million to spend, but it spent just $52.6 million, according to the National Rural Housing Coalition. The money provides direct loans to developers, nonprofits or low-income people to build multifamily units and to renew existing contracts in rural communities.

“These are programs that help people,” said Bob Rapoza, a lobbyist for the National Rural Housing Coalition. He noted that USDA obligated more in the most recent fiscal year than in previous years but that it was still lagging.

USDA has also not published requests for applications for multifamily housing programs in both fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026. The money doesn’t expire because it’s appropriated on a “no-year” basis, meaning it doesn’t have to be spent within a specific time frame. But the lack of spending is raising questions about what’s behind the delay.

USDA blamed last year's government shutdown for the delays.

"There have been reforms to the obligation system including, for the first time in the programs history, a loan committee has been created to ensure borrowers have the necessary credit to qualify and along other modernization efforts," a spokesperson told MA. "With these changes we expect obligations will increase significantly for both future funds and remaining funds which do not expire."

Key Context: The department’s Rural Development arm has faced scrutiny since Marcia first reported that it let hundreds of millions of dollars in funding for low-income housing in a different program expire. The move drew pushback from Democratic lawmakers, who asked USDA to preserve the funds.

Zoom out: Housing is becoming increasingly expensive as inflation ticks up and building costs rise. A White House from June 2025 noted that the cost of housing in rural America —typically GOP strongholds — has risen six times faster than homeowner incomes. That’s put Republicans on defense even in areas where they normally dominate.
SNAP CHATS

FIRST IN MA: State governments are short an estimated $469 million in new costs that will be needed to run SNAP, the nation’s largest food aid program, according to a report out today from MAZON, a Jewish anti-hunger group.

Republicans’ megalaw passed in July 2025 increased the state share of administrative costs for running SNAP from 50% to 75%. USDA estimates that will cost states $1.61 billion total annually. But states have enacted just $1.14 billion in extra funding for the program, according to the report.

That is putting states in “the impossible position of having to raise taxes, pull resources from other services, or drop their SNAP programs altogether,” said MAZON President and CEO Abby J. Leibman in a statement.

What’s next: States are already scrambling to prepare for the next cost-shift. As part of the megalaw, Republicans imposed new penalties on states that make administrative errors when making SNAP payments.

States with high error rates will be required to pay part of the cost of SNAP benefits for the first time at the start of fiscal 2028, which Democrats are trying to delay, and many are making huge changes to how they run the program in order to minimize those costs. Those administrative changes, in turn, are already making it more difficult for eligible people to access SNAP, contributing to a precipitous decline in participation, as Marcia previously reported.
Midterms Watch

COMMITTEE HOPEFULS: Johnny Garcia, the Democratic nominee for Texas’ 35th District, said he aspires to join the House Ag Committee if he wins against Republican Carlos De La Cruz in November.

Garcia said his ambition is motivated by concern for SNAP recipients. Food aid has been a central policy dispute between ag Democrats and Republicans, with Senate Ag Democrats uniformly opposing the farm bill because it does not delay a requirement for states to pay part of the costs of SNAP benefits.

“The Farm Bill is really big here in south central Texas,” Garcia told Cassandra. “I have a good relationship with our food banks here, and I know these communities.”

The 35th District, which stretches from Austin to San Antonio, is a "Lean R” seat on the Cook Political Report but has become “surprisingly competitive” due to affordability issues, according to the San Antonio Report.

Garcia criticized Republicans for cuts to SNAP in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“I would ask some of the school members, some of the food banks, ‘Now that the SNAP benefits have been taken away, how big are these lines?’” Garcia said. “And he says, ‘They're wrapped around the corner.’”

The 35th District was represented by Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), but he chose to run for a different seat this cycle due to redistricting.
Row Crops

— United Farm Workers criticized a recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge in California's Central Valley, and called House Ag Rep. David Valadao’s (R-Calif.) remarks on the operations “insulting.” Valadao said in a statement that the Department of Homeland Security informed him that its “operations are focused on individuals with active warrants and known criminal histories.”

— USDA announced $825 million in international food assistance investments, administered through the Food for Peace, McGovern-Dole Food for Education and Food for Progress programs.

— Those on the front lines of feeding their neighbors in West Virginia’s coal country say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. (NBC News)

item.title: Was eggflation foul play?
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Marcia Brown and Rachel Shin

With help from Steve Folk and Cheyenne Haslett

The average price of eggs in a U.S. supermarket went from $1.93 per dozen in January 2022 to $4.82 a year later. | Scott Olson/Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Economists dismissed egg collusion as crankery and blamed bird flu for high prices for years. Then the feds found evidence that could prove the cranks right.

— Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is hoping to score a buzzer-beater win on ultraprocessed foods before the November midterms.

— The School Nutrition Association is warning of a budget crisis.

IT’S MONDAY, OCT. 19. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! We’re your hosts, Marcia Brown and Rachel Shin. Send pitches and tips to marciabrown@politico.com and rshin@politico.com. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
Driving the day

ALTERNATE EGGS-PLANTION: When you see the cost of an everyday item — the kind you’re going to buy regardless of price — more than double in a year, do you get suspicious?

When it came to eggs, whose average price in a U.S. supermarket went from $1.93 per dozen in January 2022 to $4.82 a year later — and not even for the lovingly cared-for, cage-free variety — Americans had their choice of explanations.

Some supply chain experts pointed to continued pandemic-era disruptions. The geopolitically minded cited impacts of war in agriculturally productive Ukraine,shrinking global supply while driving up fuel and feed costs. Republicans blamed the Democratic administration for wild spending that prompted widespread “Bidenflation.”

Most Americans appeared content with the prevailing rationale they were given: Bird flu, an epidemic with a near-100% mortality rate,contributed to the death of 43 million egg-laying hens in 2022 alone while consumers continued to crave omelettes.

Peter Carstensen, a law school professor and fellow at the American Antitrust Institute, watched the prices of eggs rise from his Wisconsin home and suspected all those explanations were ignoring the potential for human villainy in a market where demand remains fixed.

“Eggs are a classic example of where collusion makes an awful lot of sense,” said Carstensen. “I am going to have my two eggs and bacon every Wednesday, and on Saturday as well, regardless of the price of eggs.”

The suspicion of antitrust hawks like Carstensen — that producers were choosing to raise prices in tandem to increase profits rather than competing in a way that would drive prices down — was dismissed by mainstream economists and commentators as the work of cranks looking past simple economics for a true crime story that could exist only in their minds. Washington Post columnist Megan McArdle waved away “internet memes and a fair amount of conspiracizing,”as she put it, “about monopolistic egg producers colluding to raid the pockets of hard-working, egg-loving Americans.”

Other free marketeers made it a Rorschach test of financial literacy flunked by those desperate to feed a populist cause.

“You don’t need shadowy conspiracies of egg producers to understand the dynamics of egg-flation in the United States,”agricultural economist Jeremy Horpedahl wrote on a blog for the libertarian Cato Institute. “All you need to explain the price fluctuations of eggs is good old supply and demand.”

The truth was out there. Investigators found what they considered evidence of a scheme in which three of the country’s largest egg producers coordinated inflated bids to a central price clearinghouse so as to artificially drive up prices in ways immediately felt by consumers, as the U.S. Justice Department and 17 state attorneys general outlined in a lawsuit.

It took three years for them to disentangle the alleged conspiracy, with limited consequences for the companies, which never admitted wrongdoing. The cranks, it turned out, just saw what no one else did — and the rest of us are still catching up.

Read the full piece from Marcia and Steve in POLITICO Magazine here.
MAHA MOMENT

LAST-GASP EFFORT: Kennedy is taking another run at defining ultraprocessed foods, a longtime target of his Make America Healthy Again movement.

The effort, led by the Department of Health and Human Services and involving senior White House officials, comes less than two weeks ahead of a midterm election in which turning out MAHA voters could prove pivotal for the GOP — and after months of complaints that the administration didn’t live up to its promises.

Conversations among officials have picked up in recent weeks after talks stalled this summer, said three administration officials, who were granted anonymity to describe internal discussions.

Defining ultraprocessed foods, a step the government hasn’t taken before, could redirect Americans’ diets away from foods that Kennedy and his allies blame for the country’s chronic disease epidemic. Kennedy and many MAHA advocates have called for ultraprocessed foods to carry warning labels that they believe would help people avoid harmful foods.

A higher-level meeting is scheduled for this week between Kennedy and senior White House officials to discuss the status of the food policy, two of the officials said. The revived conversations signal potential progress on one of MAHA’s top priorities at a time when Republicans are struggling to persuade voters that they’ve delivered on their campaign pledges.

Read the full story from Cheyenne and Marcia here.
FOOD PRICES AND NUTRITION

SCHOOL MEALS FUNDING CRUNCH: A coalition of farm, anti-hunger and health groups joined with SNA to urge Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to deploy more funds for school meals.

“America's school meal programs are facing a growing financial crisis,” the groups wrote in a letter sent last week to Rollins and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought. “In addition, 35 percent of school meal programs operated at a deficit at the end of School Year 2023-24, nearly double the 18 percent reported two school years earlier.”

The groups asked Rollins and Vought to use available funds in Section 32 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1935 to “provide emergency financial relief for school meal programs nationwide.” (MA readers may remember this is the same fund the Department of Agriculture tapped during last year’s government shutdown to keep afloat a federal nutrition program for low-income moms and babies.)

It comes just a month after SNA sent a letter to OMB calling on the Trump administration to tap the funds.

Context: School nutrition professionals have long argued that the federal reimbursement rate for school meals doesn’t cover the true cost but claim recent inflation has made the problem worse. Just like families at the grocery store, schools are paying more to feed their students, and they’re having to tap into their own budgets to fund it.

What’s next: A forthcoming regulation that is intended to align school meal programs with the recently updated dietary guidelines has yet to be released — and could add even more costs to school budgets.

item.title: Ag Republicans’ ICE problem
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

ICE raids are disrupting farm communities in the runup to the midterms. | Charly Triballeau/Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in farm country are creating a difficult situation for vulnerable ag Republicans to defend.

— President Donald Trump is set to lower tariffs on Canada for certain agricultural goods, after appeals from a Maine Republican.

— The Agriculture Department is partnering with NASA to improve ag data quality.

IT’S MONDAY, OCT. 26. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send pitches and tips to rshin@politico.com and contact me securely on Signal at rshin.80. Follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
Driving the day

SLIPPING ON ICE: ICE raids are disrupting farm communities in the runup to the midterms — putting Republican incumbents in a pinch as they weigh breaking with Trump or alienating some voters.

Democratic challengers are using the issue to skewer their GOP opponents in an already unfavorable political climate.

Randy Villegas, a Democrat running to unseat House Ag member David Valadao (R-Calif.), said ICE raids in his district are making farm workers afraid to go to work and stoking fears of family separation.

“Valadao said that they're only going after people with criminal records and things like that, when in fact they're targeting our farm workers who don't have any previous record,” Villegas told your host.

“They're simply targeting anyone and everyone who is here to live a better and dignified life and who actually grows the food that not only feeds the rest of the country, but feeds the rest of the world,” he said.

Valadao did not respond to a request for comment.

California's 22nd Congressional District is heavily agricultural, producing a large amount of specialty crops and dairy. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report categorizes the race as a toss-up.

Valadao acknowledged the ICE raids earlier this month in a statement, saying he was in contact with the Department of Homeland Security. He said DHS informed his office that the raids are “focused on individuals with active warrants and known criminal histories,” a statement that drew backlash from farmworker groups and Villegas.

Teresa Romero, United Farm Workers’ president, told MA that ICE’s presence has forced difficult decisions for farm workers in the area, such as parents choosing to work at two different farms so that if one parent is “picked up, there will still likely be one parent who can come home and take care of the kids.”

Over in the Sunflower State: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) is more vulnerable than expected in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost a century. And recent ICE raids in the southwestern corner of the state, which ranchers said have cost them millions, aren’t doing him any favors.

Nick Hernandez, city manager of Dodge City, one of three major beef-producing cities in southwestern Kansas, said ICE’s presence in October has been “pretty detrimental to the community,” with people staying home from work at meat processing plants and children skipping school out of fear.

Hernandez said he aired his concerns to Marshall and Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), but the lawmakers couldn’t offer assurances that ICE wouldn’t flood Dodge City again.

“They cannot assure us that it couldn't happen again, from communications with them,” Hernandez told MA. “We really do not have any answers whatsoever yet from the Department of Homeland Security.”

“We've all expressed our concerns with the enforcement action and the lack of communication that was occurring,” he added.

Marshall and Moran did not respond to a request for comment.

Matt Teagarden, CEO of the Kansas Livestock Association, said there is “concern about some of the policies from the administration” among farmers and ranchers in the state, who have voted overwhelmingly Republican in the past.

Whether rural Kansans will actually channel that frustration into votes for a Democratic Senate nominee is “the million-dollar question,” Teagarden said. Farm constituents could also stay home on election day.

“I have talked to ag producers, farmers, ranchers, cattle feeders that are going to vote different this time, no question,” Teagarden told MA. “But I think overall, there will be some that will decide to send the message a different way.”
TRADE TALKS

TRADE PLAYS: Trump will soften his tariffs on Canadian exports that are hurting Maine’s agriculture industry, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said Friday, as our Daniel Desrochers, Megan Messerly and Sue Allan report.

Collins said the Trump administration will lower its 50% tariffs on nine categories of products used by Maine’s agriculture industry, including some paper goods, plastic boxes, packing supplies, refrigeration and freezing equipment, as well as seaweed and edible algae. The change will take effect Oct. 30.

“These producers are a vital part of our state’s economy and support our rural and coastal communities,” Collins said in a statement. “Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”

A person familiar with the discussions said the overall amount of the tariffs on Canadian goods will remain unchanged — they will just be transferred to different items. The tariffs will instead hit about 100 new categories of products, including cocoa powder, shampoos, carpets, canoes and wooden coffins, according to an executive order the White House released Friday afternoon.

The person, who was granted anonymity to discuss the move, added that the goal is to give Collins an electoral win without changing the United States’ overall posture toward Canada.

It’s unclear how much the relief will improve Collins’ reelection odds. Two people familiar with the action, granted anonymity to share details of the carve-outs, said the administration is betting the move will help Collins keep her seat.

Even this late in the game, “it will help because it demonstrates her ability to fix problems for Mainers,” said one of the people, a Republican close to the White House.

While she has criticized Trump’s double-digit tariffs on neighboring Canada as well as the White House’s broader trade agenda, Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson has continued to hammer her on the issue on the campaign trail.

Jackson did not let up in a post on social media responding to the announcement Friday afternoon, saying Collins “enabled this chaos” by voting to confirm the Trump administration officials behind the tariffs, and he compared the relief to “bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”
AROUND THE AGENCIES

SHOOT FOR THE STARS: Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman are collaborating to strengthen USDA’s data quality through new technology.

Rollins and Isaacman have signed a memorandum of understanding to integrate NASA’s geospatial analytics and statistical methodologies into USDA’s ag statistics.

“With this unprecedented partnership the Trump Administration is committing to a bright future of research and tech opportunities that will enhance USDA acreage and yield estimation and drive profitability for American agriculture,” Rollins said in a statement.

Isaacman added that NASA’s earth observation data can make USDA’s understanding of crop conditions and hazards more robust. USDA and NASA plan to conduct joint technical reviews of crop yield models and the tools that generate planted and harvested area estimations.

MA readers will recall: USDA has been increasingly turning to technology to break a cycle of inaccurate crop forecasts that are eroding farmers’ willingness to participate in surveys, in turn making the reports even less reliable, as your host reported.

The trend was highlighted earlier this year when participation in a spring survey of farmers’ planting plans reached a record low, according to the National Agricultural Statistics Service, after a revised corn report in January exceeded earlier forecasts and tanked markets.

Rollins issued a request for information on how to improve the surveys earlier this year and heard critiques from farmers as she visited fairs across the country this summer. The department has responded by developing tools meant to modernize its data collection and sharing.
Row Crops

We invite our readers to attend and hear them unpack the FDA and USDA’s fall food agenda, highlighting recent and upcoming rules, guidance and policy actions. The webinar is free to attend,and you can register here.

— Rollins will host a press conference in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, today to discuss trade policy under the Trump administration.

— USDA announced the appointment of four members to its Tribal Advisory Committee and opened a call for nominations to serve on the committee.

— USDA is making up to $5 billion in loans available through the Strengthening Processing for U.S. Ranchers Guaranteed Loan Program to improve the processing capacity of meat, poultry and seafood sectors.

— The European Union’s “veggie bacon” ban spells trouble for meat-flavored chips, our Ketrin Jochecová reports.

— Zach Lahn, Iowa’s Republican gubernatorial nominee, has an unusual connection to the Koch family. (The New York Times)

— Everyone wants a bite of China’s egg tart economy. (Bloomberg)
