By Rachel Shin

Presented by 

With help from Marcia Brown

President Donald Trump gestures as he arrives to deliver remarks during a campaign rally. | Getty Images

FOLLOW ELECTION NIGHT WITH POLITICO: Track what’s happening across the country and what it means for the next two years at POLITICO.com and in our new mobile app. Then tune in at 9 p.m. ET for POLITICO Elections Live, where Alex Burns, Jonathan Martin and Playbook co-authors Dasha Burns, Adam Wren and Will Steakin break down the results in a show built for people who want the story beyond the numbers.
QUICK FIX

— The Trump administration has courted rural voters in the run-up to tomorrow’s midterm election, but some GOP strategists worry it might not be enough to overcome a poor farm economy.

— President Donald Trump spoke in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, urging his base to support Republicans and touting direct cash aid he has given growers.

— Zen Honeycutt of Moms Across America endorsed 10 Democrats in the closing days of election season, then campaigned with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

IT’S MONDAY, NOV. 2. Welcome to Morning Agriculture, and happy election-eve! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and midterms chatter to rshin@politico.com and follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

THE RURAL VOTERS QUESTION: Trump campaigned in farm states over the weekend in an eleventh-hour appeal to his rural base.

The president’s barnstorming in Iowa and Kansas Sunday was his latest effort to turn out Republican voters in agricultural areas, where economic malaise is particularly potent. Democrats and Republicans agree that Trump’s economy will be on the ballot, and some GOP strategists say the headwinds could depress turnout in farm communities and even spur some constituents to vote blue.

“You have the trade wars, and the retaliation from China and others have largely dried up international markets for things like soybeans and other row crops,” said GOP strategist Ryan Horn, who is based in Nebraska. “We set a recent historical record in farm bankruptcies last year in 2025, and we're on pace to see something similar or worse this year.”

Horn added that Election Day will indicate whether those economic blows have alienated what has been a “pretty reliable and overwhelming Republican vote over the last 10 to 15 years.”

The GOP is hoping that Trump’s stumping in ag states and recent farm policy announcements, like his allotment of $8 billion for fuel relief for growers, will goose turnout.

“President Trump is a great motivating factor for the base, specifically in rural districts,” Zach Bannon, a National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson, told MA.

“This announcement is going to bolster Republican turnout,” Bannon added. “It's going to strengthen our base, and it's going to show that this administration, along with House Republicans, are focused on delivering for rural America.”

But the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee argued the financial hits to farmers have sent a stronger message to the bloc than the recent cash aid and appearances from the president.

“I think certainly they are likely trying to staunch the bleeding, but it's a little late in the game for that, right?” DCCC spokesperson Katie Smith told MA. “Really what they're asking people to do is to ignore your eyes and ears, ignore your wallets, ignore your pocketbooks.”

About that $8 billion: Trump announced the $8 billion in relief for farmers struggling with high fuel prices in October. But growers won’t receive aid payments until at least late November or early December.

Some GOP operatives say that might not be enough to make good with alienated voters.

“My gut tells me, and the data tells me, that voters are looking at everything over the past year, in particular, and how they feel about their livelihood,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based GOP strategist and alumnus of Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) campaign staff.

“That's going to weigh much heavier than recent decisions and policies that might give a little bit of relief in the last two or three weeks before the election,” he added.

Staying on subject: While Trump was present in farm states frequently in the runup to the election, his talking points have vacillated widely.

“A lot of the clips that come out of that have been about Jon Husted's ass,” Horn said of Trump’s recent speeches. “It's a funny joke. … But it is a little bit off message.”

Steinhauser said while part of Trump’s appeal is that he is “unscripted,” he thinks the president hasn’t focused enough on “the wins of the administration.”

“He's not been on message,” Steinhauser said. “Acknowledging the pain that people feel is really important.”

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told MA in a statement that Trump is “helping our agriculture industry by negotiating new trade deals, lowering input costs, bolstering the farm safety net, doubling the death tax exemption, ending taxes on rural property loan interest, and creating rural opportunity zones.”

Kelly added that Trump “continues to talk about all of these accomplishments and more.”
 

Raphael Warnock on the midterms and Democrats’ path forward

In the latest episode of On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Sen. Raphael Warnock in Atlanta to discuss the battle for the Senate, Democrats’ prospects across the South and what he believes the party needs to build a lasting majority.

Watch now.

 
 
AROUND THE STATES

TRUMP STUMPS: Trump campaigned in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday, where he wooed producers and highlighted cash infusions he has given the farm economy.

“Nobody’s done more for farmers than Donald Trump, that I can tell you,” Trump told the crowd. “We’re giving you $12 billion. We want to get you through a little bit of a period.”

The president also highlighted that he gave farmers $28 billion in aid during his first term. He mentioned high cost-of-living issues tied to the war in Iran, saying that when the war ends, the public will “see gasoline [prices] coming down.”

He also spoke about the cost of food, saying egg prices were “literally five times higher” under the Biden administration but that “eggs are now as low as they were in my [first] administration.” The price of eggs has come down significantly from record highs in spring of 2025.

Trump also spoke in Salina, Kansas, Sunday evening. The Kansas and Iowa rallies were originally canceled last week but rescheduled on Friday.

RURAL HOUSING LATEST: Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden took to social media Friday to defend the Trump administration’s changes to a rural housing program that critics argue have led to millions of dollars in expired funds.

“USDA stands firmly by these reforms and refuses to return to high-risk operational models and backlogs of the past,” Vaden wrote in a letter to Rep. Jim Costa (D-Calif.), who had asked the Department of Agriculture for answers about funds for the Single Family Direct Home Loans program that were set to expire with the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30.

POLITICO first reported that roughly $232 million in federal dollars designed to help low-income rural communities buy homes were set to return to the Treasury because they hadn’t yet been spent by the Rural Development agency, a move USDA blamed on last year’s record-setting government shutdown.

MAHA MOMENT

CRACKS IN THE COALITION: One of Kennedy’s most prominent supporters is making good on her threat to endorse some Democrats days before the midterm elections, our Cheyenne Haslett and Amanda Friedman report.

The Democrats on Honeycutt’s list aren’t just any Democrats.

Her Moms Across America Movement is backing progressive firebrands such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), as well as candidates in crucial battlegrounds, like Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.), who’s running for Senate.  

Kennedy has urged his supporters to stick with Republicans. But if MAHA advocates follow Honeycutt’s lead, it could undermine his efforts.

Honeycutt is making the case that Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement needs to support candidates who get behind his plans to restrict pesticides and make food healthier, regardless of party, if it wants to see policies change.

“We expect Democrats and Republicans to work together. Health is not a political issue. You know, poison is not partisan. Cancer is not choosy,” Honeycutt said.

“We can all work together to Make America Healthy Again, whether you call it that or not,” Honeycutt told POLITICO.

Her group has also backed dozens of Republicans and independents — the majority of its endorsements — and Honeycutt hasn’t pared back her support for Kennedy.

She took the stage at a MAHA rally last week in Iowa with the health secretary, and the state’s Republican candidate for governor, Zach Lahn, urging the crowd to support Lahn in the midterm elections. Lahn has centered his campaign on MAHA issues, including pesticide exposure and water quality, which he links to Iowa’s high cancer rates.

But for months, MAHA activists have warned that they could abandon the MAGA-MAHA alliance if they don’t see progress on the issues they care about. Honeycutt is particularly disappointed with actions taken by Trump, such as his move this year to boost production of the key ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup.

“The Republicans were supportive of this MAHA movement, but most of the Republicans in office did not follow through with the promises that we were given, especially around pesticides, and so they are losing a huge opportunity to Make America Healthy Again,” Honeycutt said.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by Bayer: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin and Grace Yarrow

Presented by Bayer

With help from Marcia Brown

A top USDA adviser recently said fertilizer producers are being “unfairly” demonized. | Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP
QUICK FIX

— A top Agriculture Department adviser’s fertilizer defense infuriated USDA officials and farm groups.

— A $100 million plan to turn the Make America Healthy Again movement into a Republican turnout machine collapsed into canceled rallies and unfunded candidates.

— A group representing elected ag officials is urging USDA to approve bird flu vaccines for cattle.

IT’S MONDAY, NOV. 9. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, contact me securely on Signal at rshin.80 and follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Bayer:

At Bayer, we empower American farms with the smart tools needed to advance regenerative agriculture. By providing accurate, real-time data maps, we give farmers necessary insights to improve soil health and protect the land for generations. When farmers are equipped to care for their soil with tools like real-data maps, stronger yields and a sustainable bottom line naturally follow. Learn more.
 
Driving the day

GOING OFF SCRIPT? Trump administration officials who spent months trying to shore up their support among farmers on a suite of economic issues are now finding themselves at odds with a critic in their own ranks.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins has moved to reduce reliance on foreign fertilizer companies while other federal agencies investigate whether those companies engage in illegal anti-competitive business practices. But Kip Tom, a Rollins adviser, recently countered the administration’s message by saying fertilizer producers are being “unfairly” demonized.

Tom’s defense of the fertilizer industry in a letter to the leader of a major corn grower group and a September opinion piece angered corn farmers and blindsided Trump officials, according to four people with direct knowledge of the conversations and granted anonymity to discuss them.

And his words fueled perceptions among these officials that Tom is motivated by a potential business opportunity: He mentioned his interest in purchasing fertilizer production facilities, including from industry giant Nutrien, at a formal meeting and an event in recent months, said the four people, who also had direct knowledge of those interactions.

Tom, who advises Rollins as a temporary government employee helping modernize USDA data, denies discussing investments with Nutrien and having any commercial investments in fertilizer production. He told POLITICO he “was aware of” a Nutrien plant and other facilities operating below capacity that could provide “diverse solutions” to the U.S. fertilizer supply.

A Nutrien spokesperson did not address POLITICO’s questions about whether Tom made any business inquiry, only saying the company is “well-positioned to continue meeting customer demand through our North American nitrogen operations.”

Tom’s clash with farmers over high fertilizer prices had undercut the Trump administration's effort to show solidarity with rural communities heading into the midterm election, said one of the people.

“He's absolutely working against the interests of the Trump administration,” said the person. “He's gone rogue.”

Get all the juicy details from Grace here.
 

Raphael Warnock predicts a blue Mississippi

In the latest episode of On the Road, Sen. Raphael Warnock sits down with Jonathan Martin in Atlanta to make his case for investing in Mississippi, South Carolina and other Southern states as Democrats look to build a lasting majority.

Watch now.

 
 
MAHA MOMENT


A RUDE AWAKENING: Despite massive early donations to the MAHA movement’s leading campaign vehicle — and promises from movement leader Tony Lyons that MAHA PAC would donate $100 million to aligned Republicans — the group struggled to raise money and distribute it to candidates.

Federal filings show Lyons-led committees have spent under $3.5 million on its candidates, with just over $1.2 million in competitive congressional races. Not a dollar went to support Andy Biggs, the Republican candidate for governor, even though he had MAHA PAC’s endorsement.

The group ended up canceling two of the three rallies on an October campaign tour it had announced to help candidates.

By Election Day, many activists were accusing the Trump administration of betrayal. The presidential candidate who championed MAHA issues from his campaign podium in 2024 had not gone far enough on those policies as president, in some cases even taking them in the opposite direction, they said, most notably by backing pesticide producer Bayer before the Supreme Court as it fought allegations that its product Roundup causes cancer.

The policy decisions were devastating to MAHA supporters who wanted to see pesticides eliminated from the food system.

“What we saw in 2024 is that MAHA issues do drive people to the ballot box. The problem is that if you drop the ball on implementing them, MAHA enthusiasts lose their enthusiasm,” said Patrick Sullivan, a MAHA supporter and co-founder of Firefly Organic Coffee and Market in Scottsdale, Arizona, where patrons can order pumpkin lattes infused with collagen and topped off with raw milk.

Credited with helping to propel President Donald Trump to victory in 2024, MAHA issues were priorities in few federal races this year, and related PACs never became the kind of political money machine that could help elect movement-friendly lawmakers.

“The MAHA story is a case study and a proof point of the overarching story of the midterms, which is the rug pull,” said Calley Means, a Kennedy ally who served as a senior adviser in the Department of Health and Human Services until abruptly resigning shortly before the election and airing sharp criticism of the White House. “Voters felt rug-pulled on almost every part of the Republican agenda. MAHA is one proof point in that.”

Read the full story from our Catherine Kim, Amanda Chu, Cheyenne Haslett and Marcia here.
 

A message from Bayer:
 

NO LOVE LOST: Means torched now-former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and several of Trump’s top advisers last week, laying the blame at their feet for stalled progress on populist platforms, Cheyenne, Marcia and Lauren Gardner report.

In an episode of the popular “Joe Rogan Experience” podcast that aired Friday, Means said Wiles, deputy chief of staff Richard Walters, assistant to the president for policy Walker Barrett, top political strategist James Blair and Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio killed the MAHA movement’s momentum and stalled the priorities that he believes Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. were ushered into Washington to deliver.

“These people just, and I don’t mean this like in a really dismissive way, these aren’t the best and brightest, these staffers. They have tremendous power, though,” Means told Rogan, who has often promoted the MAHA movement.

Means suggested Trump fire them all.

“I would recommend that he clear his house, and I think he’s getting there,” Means said.

Download the new POLITICO app.

 
 
In the States

BIRD FLU WATCH: The National Association of State Departments of Agriculture and the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials met with USDA and urged the department to authorize a bird flu vaccination framework for dairy cattle.

The nonpartisan groups said the call came in response to ongoing bird flu outbreaks.

“The dairy industry must have effective tools to combat HPAI,” NASDA CEO Ted McKinney said in a statement. “An integrated disease control strategy must go beyond biosecurity and movement controls. … That’s why we are asking USDA to approve vaccines as an additional tool to help prevent and reduce the spread of HPAI in livestock.”

NASDA and NASAHO said while the commercial milk supply is safe, continued bird flu outbreaks threaten supply chains and international market access, which could affect the economic stability of dairy and poultry farms.

The groups wrote in the letter that persistent outbreaks could also “amplify concerns about affordability of dairy, beef, eggs and poultry products at a time when grocery prices are on the rise.”

The appeal from elected agriculture officials comes after Rachel and Marcia reported that USDA shelved an internal bird flu vaccine strategy in deference to Kennedy’s anti-vaccine views. That move ran counter to urges from Republicans and industry leaders to ensure the United States is prepared for a surge in cases this fall.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and Megafire Action: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and Megafire Action

With help from Oliver Ward

President Donald Trump tapped Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff. | Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
QUICK FIX

— House Ag Republicans say they hope the new White House chief of staff’s deportation agenda will not destabilize the farm workforce.

— Democrats urged Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to use “all the tools at your disposal” to help school meal programs that are financially underwater.

— The Agriculture Department delayed new stocking standards after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged the president to push the enactment back.

IT’S MONDAY, NOV. 16. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, contact me securely on Signal at rshin.80 and follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and Megafire Action:

Wildfires don’t wait for Congress. 50+ organizations call on Congress to pass the bipartisan Fix Our Forests Act before the end of the year, from fire chiefs and state foresters to ranchers, insurers, conservation groups and the business community. In 2026, more than 66,000 wildfires burned over 9 million acres. It’s time for action. Let’s get it done. Read the letter: https://alliancewr.org/fofaletter
 
Driving the day

THE NEW BOSS: Ag Republicans said they hope Stephen Miller’s ascension to White House chief of staff won’t mean an escalation of the deportation tactics that have made it harder for farmers to maintain a stable workforce.

“It's clear out there what's going on in the ag world. We need the labor force,” Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) told MA. “[Miller] assured me at one point that all of their efforts to remove people from the country that are here illegally would not focus on the agricultural labor force, and so, [I] would like to remind him of that.”

Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) said that early in the second Trump administration, Miller told him that he saw some visa and workforce programs in other countries that were “effective and helpful and had a lot of integrity.”

“I would ask him and the president to work with Congress to design something that really recognizes the importance of, you know, these workforce programs,” Moolenaar said, naming the H-2A farm guest worker visa program as one example.

Some Republicans keen on expanding farm labor pathways said President Donald Trump’s softened comments on immigration last week are a good sign that Miller will support stabilizing the farm workforce.

“I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs — that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally,” the president said in an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes,” adding that his deportation policy was “too tough.”

House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) noted to your host that Trump “indicated that we have a need for an agricultural workforce. I suspect that he sought Mr. Miller's opinion on that before he made those remarks.”

Newhouse added that Trump’s recent comments may signal an opening for a “compromise deal on solving some of our labor issues in the ag world.”

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, told MA in a statement that the Trump administration’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged: the Administration will continue to keep our southern border secure and prioritize removing the worst of the worst from our country.”

“While keeping the President’s promise to enforce our immigration laws, the Administration is ensuring all sectors — including farmers — have the resources and legal workforce they need to be successful,” Rogers added.

John Hollay, president and CEO of the National Council of Agricultural Employers, said Miller has the opportunity to advance the president’s farm labor agenda by supporting legislation that would codify the Trump administration's Adverse Effect Wage Rates interim final rule, a policy that cut the minimum wage for migrant farm workers but was blocked by a judge.

“First and foremost, the Chief of Staff has demonstrated that his top priority is the success of President Trump,” Hollay told MA in a statement, adding that Trump signaled publicly that “he remains committed to not disrupting the essential workforces that are critical to our economy.”
 

A message from the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and Megafire Action:
 
ON THE HILL

MA EXCLUSIVE: House Education and the Workforce Committee ranking member Bobby Scott (D-Va.) and Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) are pushing Rollins to support school meals programs that are in financial crisis.

The Democrats said in a letter Sunday that the rates for federal reimbursements administered by USDA have not kept up with rising costs. They added that cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in the GOP’s megalaw, passed in summer 2025, damaged eligibility for low-income students to receive free or reduced-price meals.

“We implore you to use all the tools at your disposal to better support child nutrition programs that are struggling,” the lawmakers wrote, adding that they want Rollins to “reflect the need for any authority or additional funding for child nutrition programs in the President’s budget proposal.”

Scott and DeLauro said school meals programs’ financial plight inhibits districts from enacting the Trump administration’s Make America Healthy Again standards, such as using whole and unprocessed ingredients, in meals.

“Meal providers cannot rise to the occasion of meeting higher standards while also operating on shoestring margins,” the Democrats said.

A USDA spokesperson told MA in a statement that "any assertion that H.R. 1 cut school meal eligibility or diminishes schools’ ability to offer free meals are incorrect."

"The statutory changes to SNAP do not alter the eligibility rules or operational requirements governing the National School Lunch Program or School Breakfast Program, including the Community Eligibility Provision," the spokesperson added.

 

A message from the Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and Megafire Action:

Right now, there are firefighters waiting on tools that Congress has already negotiated. It’s just a matter of voting. The Fix Our Forests Act would improve real-time decision-making, speed fuels reduction where homes meet wildland, expand prescribed fire and help communities become more resilient. In 2026, more than 66,000 wildfires burned over 9 million acres. That’s why more than 50 organizations have asked congressional leaders to pass the bill before the end of the year. They include cattle producers, public lands ranchers, state foresters, hunters and anglers, rural conservation groups and wildland firefighters. Read the letter: https://alliancewr.org/fofaletter
 
NEW YORK CITY

MAMDANI SECURES DELAY: The Trump administration is granting the nation’s grocery and convenience stores a 90-day reprieve before they must comply with a new regulation that will require them to broaden the range of foods they sell to accept federal food aid benefits as payment, our Grace Yarrow and Marcia Brown report.

The delay, announced by USDA Friday, comes after Mamdani brokered a deal with Trump to give stores a cushion before they must stock more varieties of fruits, dairy, vegetables and grains in order to accept SNAP benefits. Mamdani warned the Trump administration in a letter earlier this month that the pending rule would hurt the city’s bodegas and corner stores.

The mayor said he escalated the extension request to the president after sending the letter.

“What I told the president was that this is a rule that, if allowed to be implemented on the timeline as it was scheduled, would be one that would throw the lives of so many working New Yorkers into a real place of anxiety and chaos,” Mamdani said during a news conference announcing the change. “And the president took that concern seriously.”

USDA officials have resisted lobbying campaigns from groups — including the National Association of Convenience Stores and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners — to push the regulation’s implementation date by six months, according to three people familiar with the push, who were granted anonymity to discuss the efforts.

A group of Republican senators also urged USDA to give retailers more time to comply, and some anti-hunger groups have argued that the new regulations will restrict options for SNAP participants because some retailers will opt out of the program entirely.

“The convenience store lobby spent millions fighting policy that ensures children have access to more healthy foods, instead of demanding their members comply,” a USDA spokesperson said in a statement on Friday. “Today, the Department will afford retailers 90 more days to get it right. Recipients, regardless of zip code and community, should have access to more than jelly and meat sticks.”
TRADE TALKS

COUNTING SHEEP: The International Trade Commission is divided on whether rising lamb meat imports, primarily from Australia and New Zealand, are significantly hurting the U.S. industry, but it said the investigation will still proceed, Oliver reports.

In a 3-3 vote on Friday, the ITC commissioners were evenly split. In the event of a tie vote, the investigation continues and the ITC prepares a report with proposed remedies for the president. It will be up to Trump whether he takes remedial action, such as enacting new tariffs.

That report is due by Jan. 11, 2027.

“While we would have preferred a clear affirmative decision, a tie still results in an important step forward for American sheep producers,” Ben Lehfeldt, board president at the American Sheep Industry, said in a statement.
Row Crops

— Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) and ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) announced the committee will hold a business meeting today in conjunction with evening votes to consider the nominations of Greg Ibach to be undersecretary of Agriculture for trade and foreign agricultural affairs and three other nominees to be members of the Farm Credit Administration board.

— Boozman and Klobuchar announced the Ag Committee will hold a hearing tomorrow at 3 p.m. to consider nominees to be commissioners of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

— Senate Health Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said Sunday that he still has questions about Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration, leaving the outcome of Wednesday’s HELP Committee vote uncertain, our Jalen Beckford reports.

— A liberal Brooklyn food co-op boycotts Israeli products, and New Jersey regulators are scrutinizing it, our Daniel Han reports.

Presented by Humane World Action Fund: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow and Rachel Shin

Presented by 

With help from Marcia Brown 

“By opposing Section 12006 you are effectively saying that you support California dictating agricultural policies across the country,” House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) wrote. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— The House Ag chair pushed back on two Republicans’ criticism of  efforts to add the Save Our Bacon Act to the Senate farm bill. The provision is one of the major remaining sticking points in farm bill talks.

— Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his ally Calley Means are attempting to force the EPA to regulate a pesticide that the president has gone out of his way to protect.

— High food and fuel prices are challenging federal nutrition programs for seniors.

IT’S MONDAY, NOV. 23. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, contact me securely on Signal at rshin.80, and follow us at @rachel_shin_, @YarrowGrace and @Marcia_Brown9 for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

A message from Humane World Action Fund:

California’s Prop 12—upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court—addresses the cruel confinement of mother pigs, egg-laying hens and veal calves as part of a broader shift toward improving animal welfare standards. Yet Big Pork and a few allies in Congress are pushing federal “fixes” to erase Prop 12 and related laws in 14 other states, undermining voters, farmers and fair markets. Learn more.
 
Driving the day

FIRST IN MA: House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) rebutted arguments from his GOP colleagues that preempting Proposition 12 in the farm bill would be “dangerous federal overreach.”

Thompson told Sens.Rick Scott (R-Fla.) and Susan Collins (R-Maine) that their criticism of his effort to add language from the Save Our Bacon Act to the Senate farm bill is “inaccurate” in a new letter obtained exclusively by MA.

The Ag chair argued that California’s Proposition 12, which restricts sales of out-of-state products that don’t meet the state's livestock housing standards, unfairly makes producers in other states comply with California’s rules to access its market. He also rejected their assertions that the language would benefit Smithfield Foods, a Chinese-owned company.

“By opposing Section 12006 you are effectively saying that you support California dictating agricultural policies across the country. Surely that isn’t what your constituents in Florida and Maine would want to hear,” Thompson wrote.

Thompson’s reply comes after Collins and Scott sent a letter to him and Senate Agriculture Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) Friday opposing talks about inserting the Save Our Bacon Act into the Senate farm bill.

“States’ rights are not something Washington should negotiate away,” Scott and Collins wrote.

The Republicans’ conflicting views on the preemption create another hurdle to getting the farm bill through Congress at a crucial juncture for the measure as working days peter out. The Save Our Bacon Act was included in the House-passed farm bill but excluded from the Senate’s version and has emerged as a sticking point, Boozman said in an interview Wednesday.

“We’re working on it and trying to find a compromise,” Boozman said. “There’s lots of Republicans that are very much in favor [of it], and I still haven’t found a single Democrat who is willing to support it.”

Key context: The National Pork Producers Council and Republicans from top pork-producing states, like Iowa, have pushed for years to pass federal language to preempt states from introducing requirements like Proposition 12.

Efforts to undo states’ ability to implement such guidelines have drawn fierce opposition from animal rights groups, farmers who already made changes to comply and even some Republicans who pushed to strip the language from the House version.

Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), one of two candidates to take the Senate Ag gavel next Congress, has insisted the farm bill avoid cutting conservation funds or “reopening debates” about the Proposition 12 language, which he said has “already proven too divisive to resolve.”

Bennet and other lawmakers are hoping to secure a new farm bill deal this year, and Senate Republicans are eyeing any stopgap funding package as a critical opportunity to attach farm bill language before the end of the lame duck.

That leaves them with just weeks to hammer out details of the bill or pass another extension of the 2018 version for the fourth year in a row. President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post Thursday that Republicans “MUST PASS A NEW FARM BILL DURING THE REMAINING DAYS OF CONGRESS.”

Democrats have demanded that any farm bill deal also include a two-year delay of a requirement for states to pay a portion of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.

Thompson told POLITICO last week that he’s open to giving states more time before the cost-share mandate kicks in — in exchange for adding language to address Proposition 12.
 

A message from Humane World Action Fund:
 
ON THE HILL

MA EXCLUSIVE: The United Food and Commercial Workers International Union is endorsing Rep. Shontel Brown (D-Ohio) for House Ag chair, according to a letter sent to the House Democratic Caucus today.

The union, which represents workers in food sectors including the grocery, meatpacking and food processing industries, said Brown has a “practical” leadership style they believe will foster bipartisan wins for workers.

“Representative Brown has demonstrated consistent commitment to workers’ rights, protecting access to affordable and nutritious food, and strengthening rural communities,” wrote Milton L. Jones, UFCW’s international president.

Brown is running against Reps. Don Davis (D-N.C.) and Jim Costa (D-Calif.).
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PAPER TRAIL: A scientific paper requested by Kennedy and Means took another shot at one of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s biggest goals.

The paper, which was posted on a public research repository Friday, lays out the existing scientific research linking glyphosate, the main ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, with cancer. The paper has not yet gone through the standard scientific review process, including peer review and publication in a scientific journal.

Its timing is aimed at forcing the Trump administration to more stringently regulate the chemical, a top target of MAHA activists. The EPA, which oversees pesticide approvals, is in the process of reviewing health research on glyphosate, and today is the deadline for scientific studies to be considered.

The study "really backs EPA into a corner," Means argued in an interview. Means resigned from the Department of Health and Human Services last month, citing frustration with a lack of progress on MAHA’s priorities.

The move stands to reignite the brawl within the Trump administration over an issue that pits Kennedy and MAHA activists against the president’s traditional farm and business allies.

The paper comes amid a major realignment of power within the White House, after chief of staff Susie Wiles departed following Republicans’ midterm losses and Stephen Miller, a MAHA ally, took over her role.

The White House did not reply to a request for comment on the new paper.

EPA spokesperson Cora Mandy said the agency "is aware” of the HHS review and “will evaluate it the same way we evaluate every study." She pushed back against Means' characterization that the study will force the EPA’s hand.

"We want as much high-quality research in the record as possible,” Mandy said. “Every relevant, quality study gets a seat at the table, and this one is no exception. We're working hand in hand with our HHS colleagues."

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said the reviews have been presented to an EPA-HHS work group and acknowledged that the "EPA retains responsibility for regulatory decisions."

Read the full story from our Ellie Borst and Cheyenne Haslett here.

NUTRITION FUNDING WOES: If there’s a pot of money, someone wants it.

USDA Section 32, an account that is often used to purchase American-grown foods, has a lot of extra money in it this year — and some are hoping those extra dollars can be used to help federal nutrition programs in a budget crisis. The School Nutrition Association called on the Trump administration to tap the fund this fall to support school meals programs, and this month, Meals on Wheels America President and CEO Ellie Hollander sent a letter urging the same to support the Older Americans Act Nutrition Program, which includes Meals on Wheels, among other programs.

Federal funding has not kept pace with growing need in Meals on Wheels, which has been exacerbated as people lose access to SNAP and food prices increase, explained Josh Protas, chief advocacy and policy officer at Meals on Wheels America. One in 3 of the program’s providers has a wait list, which is on average four months, Protas said.

Senate Republicans’ Labor-HHS funding bill proposes a $10 million increase in the senior nutrition programs, which Protas said is “encouraging” but falls short of what’s needed. MA readers will also remember that USDA made a significant USDA Section 32 purchase days before the November midterms.

The White House Office of Management and Budget did not respond to a request for comment.

A message from Humane World Action Fund:

The Big Pork lobby and a few congressional allies continue to make contrived arguments against California’s Prop 12, which prohibits in-state production and sale of food products from mother pigs, egg-laying chickens and veal calves locked in cruel and extreme confinement. They won’t stop until they nullify Prop 12 and related laws in 14 other states like Florida, Arizona and Ohio through federal legislation such as the Save Our Bacon Act.

Congress could soon decide whether the dangerous Save Our Bacon Act is included in the Farm Bill or other year-end legislative packages. That could wipe out important state animal protection laws like Prop 12, limit states’ ability to address some of the cruelest practices on factory farms, and overturn hundreds of other state laws on food labeling, disease prevention and quarantine control. Learn more.
 
Row Crops

— USDA told states that they can recalculate their SNAP payment error rates, a move that could reduce the cost-share burden states will be required to meet next year, Marcia reports.

— Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins posted a Bible verse on her official X account after a federal judge ordered her to stop sending Christian emails and statements to USDA's employees in her official capacity. A USDA spokesperson told MA in a statement that “there is nothing in the court order about her ability to share her faith with the public, a long-standing tradition in American government.”
